messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kaius had always taken pride in his work as a graphic designer, but after that fateful night two years ago, everything changed. He had been driving home from a late-night shift when he was pulled over by the police for a minor infraction. What ensued was a brutal and unprovoked beating at the hands of the officers, leaving Kaius with severe injuries and a deep sense of trauma. As he recalled that night, Kaius's mind would flood with unwanted thoughts – images of his own battered face staring back at him, the crunching sound of bones breaking, and the feeling of helplessness as he lay on the ground. These intrusive memories would hit him without warning, triggered by something as mundane as a visible injury or wound on someone else, be it in real life or even on TV. The sight would instantly transport him back to that fateful night, leaving him overwhelmed with emotion. In an attempt to avoid these distressing thoughts, Kaius had developed a few strategies. He spent hours scrolling through his phone, playing games, or browsing the internet – anything to distract himself from the memories and emotions that threatened to engulf him. Social interactions became increasingly difficult for him; he began avoiding people altogether, including close friends and family members. Even at work, he found it challenging to collaborate with colleagues, opting instead to focus on solo projects. Kaius's daily life was now defined by a constant sense of threat. He could never fully relax, even in the safety of his own home or office, always on high alert for potential danger. His body remained perpetually tense and ready to react, like a coiled spring waiting to be triggered. Before entering any new space, he would meticulously scan the area for possible escape routes – a habit that had become second nature. When attempting to recount the events of that fateful night, Kaius struggled to put his thoughts into words. He'd start strong but soon lose his train of thought, unable to articulate the details without becoming overwhelmed by emotion. It was as if the memories were too raw, too painful to confront head-on. The trauma had fundamentally altered Kaius's worldview. Nothing seemed meaningful anymore – not his work, not his relationships, nothing. He felt like a part of him had been irreparably destroyed, leaving behind only anger and resentment. What happened that night was deeply unjust, and the fact that no one had been held accountable gnawed at him constantly. Kaius's wife, Rachel, had tried to be supportive, but even she couldn't fully grasp the extent of his suffering. As Kaius became increasingly withdrawn, their relationship began to fray. His lack of intimacy, both physical and emotional, was starting to take its toll on their marriage. It was this realization – that he risked losing the one person who truly cared for him – that finally brought Kaius to seek help. Sitting in his therapist's office, Kaius felt a mix of trepidation and hope. He was terrified of confronting the memories and emotions he'd been avoiding for so long but also desperate to reclaim some semblance of control over his life. As he looked at the blank canvas in front of him – a stark reminder of his abandoned passion for graphic design – Kaius knew that this journey would be arduous, but he was willing to face it head-on, no matter how daunting the task seemed.
